units.title: Comparatives and superlatives
notes: Short adjectives: add -er or -est: tall, taller, the tallest. Double the last letter in big, bigger, the biggest.
Adjectives ending in -y change y to i: noisy, noisier, the noisiest.
Long adjectives: use more or the most: intelligent, more intelligent, the most intelligent.
Irregular: good, better, the best; bad, worse, the worst. Use than after a comparative: Ana is taller than me.

items.q: Our new neighbours are ___ than the old ones. We can't sleep!
items.why: noisy: change y to i and add -er

items.q: Lucia is the ___ girl in our class. She always gets top marks.
items.why: long adjective after the: the most + adjective

items.q: My grandad's beard is ___ than my dad's.
This is the ___ film I have ever seen. I hated it!
Tom is friendlier ___ his sister.
Your achievement is ___ than mine. Well done!
Marta is ___ cheerful person I know.
items.why: superlatives need the: the most cheerful

items.q: Dad's moustache is ___ than Uncle Ben's.
Who is the ___ student in your school?
My sister is ___ (bossy) than my mum. She tells everybody what to do.
items.why: bossy: y changes to i, then -er

items.q: Walking backwards is ___ (difficult) than walking forwards.
Winning the race was the ___ (good) achievement of my life.
I was nervous before the test, but Carla was even ___ (nervous) than me.
items.why: nervous is a long adjective: more nervous

items.q: An elephant has the ___ (big) teeth of all land animals.
Today the pavement is ___ (wet) than yesterday because it rained all night.
My cousin is more tall than my uncle.
a: My cousin is taller than my uncle.

items.q: She is the friendliest girl of the class.
a: She is the friendliest girl in the class.
items.why: after a superlative we say in the class

items.q: This exercise is easier that the last one.
a: This exercise is easier than the last one.

items.q: the noisiest / in / is / Leo / person / our family
a: Leo is the noisiest person in our family.
The noisiest person in our family is Leo.

items.q: he / than / is / more / cheerful / me / much
a: He is much more cheerful than me.

units.title: Present simple: affirmative, negative and questions
notes: With he, she and it add -s or -es: A seal swims. An octopus catches fish.
Negatives: don't or doesn't + base verb: Crabs don't have fins. A shark doesn't have legs.
Questions: Do or Does + subject + base verb: Does a penguin fly? No, it doesn't.
Use the present simple for facts and habits: Penguins live in cold places.

items.q: An octopus ___ eight tentacles.
items.why: an octopus is it, so has

items.q: Sharks ___ through their gills.
___ a crab walk sideways?
items.why: a crab is it, so Does

items.q: A snake ___ have legs.
Do seals eat fish? Yes, they ___.
items.why: short answer with they: they do

items.q: Penguins ___ fly, but they swim very well.
My little brother ___ sharks on TV every Saturday.
Where ___ penguins live?
Does a crab ___ a hard shell?
items.why: after Does use the base verb

items.q: Does a seal ___ (use) its flippers to swim? Yes, it does.
My dad is afraid of snakes. He ___ (not like) their fangs.
A crab ___ (catch) its food with its pincers.
Fish ___ (not have) eyelashes.
items.why: fish here is plural: don't have

items.q: The baby penguin ___ (cry) when it is hungry.
items.why: cry: y changes to i, then -es

items.q: Our teacher always ___ (go) to the aquarium with Year 5 in May.
A penguin have a black and white body.
a: A penguin has a black and white body.
items.why: a penguin is it, so has

items.q: Does sharks have sharp teeth?
My cat doesn't likes fish.
a: My cat does not like fish.
items.why: after doesn't use the base verb

items.q: don't / in / penguins / live / hot / places
a: Penguins don't live in hot places.

items.q: does / have / how many / an octopus / tentacles
a: How many tentacles does an octopus have?
items.why: How many + noun + does + subject + verb

units.title: Zero conditional
notes: If or When + present simple, present simple: If you touch fire, you get burnt.
Use it for things that are always true.
The if part can go first or second. Use a comma only when it goes first: Wool gets smaller if you wash it in hot water.
Remember the -s with he, she and it: If it rains, Dad takes an umbrella.

items.q: If you wash a wool jumper in hot water, it ___ smaller.
When it rains, I always ___ my raincoat.
If you ___ a belt, loose trousers fall down.
Silk ___ soft if you touch it.
When my dad goes to work, he ___ a suit and a tie.
If people ___ pay their taxes, the government gets angry.
Leather shoes ___ longer if you clean them every week.
My shoes hurt my feet when they ___ new.
If a button ___ off, Grandma sews it on again.
items.why: a button is it, so comes

items.q: If you ___ (not wear) a coat in winter, you feel cold.
When my sister ___ (have) a cold, she always carries a handkerchief.
items.why: my sister is she, so has

items.q: Cotton clothes ___ (dry) quickly if you hang them in the sun.
If it ___ (snow), my mum always gives me a wool scarf.
When you open an umbrella indoors, my grandad always ___ (say) it is bad luck.
If my brother ___ (not find) his pyjamas, he sleeps in a sweatshirt.
If you will press this button, the light comes on.
a: If you press this button, the light comes on.

items.q: When it is sunny, she wear a cotton dress.
a: When it is sunny, she wears a cotton dress.

items.q: If you don't wear a raincoat, you gets wet.
a: If you don't wear a raincoat, you get wet.

items.q: tight / if / hurts / my collar / is / my neck / too
a: If my collar is too tight, my neck hurts.
My neck hurts if my collar is too tight.

items.q: when / leggings / she / wears / does sport / my sister
a: When my sister does sport, she wears leggings.
My sister wears leggings when she does sport.
When she does sport, my sister wears leggings.

units.title: Modal verbs: must, mustn't, should, can, may
notes: Modal + base verb, with no to and no -s: She must go. He should listen.
Use must for rules and mustn't for things that are prohibited: You must take off your shoes. You mustn't shout.
Use should and shouldn't for advice: You should apologise. You shouldn't yawn in class.
Use can or may for permission, and may for possibility: May I come in? It may rain.

items.q: In Japan you ___ take off your shoes before you go into a house. It's a rule.
items.why: a rule is an obligation: must

items.q: You ___ yawn in front of your teacher. It's rude.
items.why: it is a bad idea, so shouldn't

items.q: She should ___ for being late.
Excuse me, ___ I sit here, please?
He ___ bow when he meets people in Thailand.
items.why: modals have no -s and no to

items.q: You ___ talk with your mouth full. It's bad manners.
items.why: the negative of must is mustn't

items.q: Take an umbrella. It ___ rain this afternoon.
You look tired. You ___ go to bed early tonight.
Must we ___ hands with everybody at the party?
In Great Britain you ___ (must) drive on the left. It's the law.
Phones are prohibited in class. You ___ (must) use your phone here.
Eating with your hands is bad manners here. You ___ (should) use a knife and fork.
items.why: advice about the right thing: should

items.q: Your friend is sad because of your words. You ___ (should) say things like that.
items.why: it is a bad idea, so shouldn't

items.q: Anna is from Belgium. She can ___ (speak) French and Dutch.
He may ___ (be) Canadian, but I'm not sure.
You must to say thank you.
She cans speak Japanese.
You don't should yawn at the table.
a: You shouldn't yawn at the table.
You should not yawn at the table.
items.why: the negative is shouldn't, without don't

items.q: shake / when / should / hands / you / meet / you / somebody
a: You should shake hands when you meet somebody.
When you meet somebody, you should shake hands.

items.q: wear / in / mustn't / the house / you / your shoes
a: You mustn't wear your shoes in the house.
In the house you mustn't wear your shoes.

units.title: Questions and question words; Present passive
notes: Question word + do or does + subject + base verb: Where does the chef work?
With be, put be before the subject: Who is that woman? Use Whose for possession: Whose bag is this?
Present passive: am, is or are + past participle: Buildings are designed by architects.
Use by to say who does the action: Bread is made by bakers.

items.q: ___ does the restaurant open? At one o'clock.
items.why: the answer is a time, so When

items.q: ___ is that woman? She's the new judge.
___ guitar is this? It's the musician's.
How ___ sailors work on this ship?
What ___ a chemist do?
items.why: a chemist is he or she: does

items.q: Medicines ___ by chemists.
The kitchen ___ every night after dinner.
items.why: the kitchen doesn't clean, somebody cleans it

items.q: This bank is managed ___ a very good banker.
Where ___ these violins made?
items.why: passive question: are + plural subject + participle

items.q: What time ___ (do) the waiters arrive at the restaurant?
How often ___ (do) your hairdresser cut your hair?
items.why: your hairdresser is he or she: does

items.q: The elderly customers ___ (serve) first in this restaurant every day.
items.why: the waiters serve them: passive, plural

items.q: Hair ___ (cut) by hairdressers.
English ___ (speak) in many countries.
Houses ___ (not build) by judges. They are built by builders.
Where works your father?
items.why: questions need does + subject + base verb

items.q: The dinner is cook by the chef.
a: The dinner is cooked by the chef.

items.q: Who's bag is this?
items.why: Who's means who is; Whose is for possession

items.q: are / by / designed / architects / new buildings
a: New buildings are designed by architects.

items.q: does / work / the detective / why / at night
a: Why does the detective work at night?

units.title: Already, still and yet; Reported speech
notes: already goes in affirmative sentences, between have and the past participle: I have already tried kayaking.
yet goes at the end of negatives and questions: She hasn't arrived yet. still goes before haven't or hasn't: We still haven't been skydiving.
Reported speech: the verb goes one step back and pronouns change: 'I like yoga,' said Ana. Ana said she liked yoga.
Reported orders: told + person + to or not to + verb: He told us to wait. He told us not to move.

items.q: I've ___ bought a souvenir, so I don't need another one.
items.why: affirmative, between have and participle: already

items.q: We haven't tried snowboarding ___.
It's ten o'clock and Tom ___ hasn't got up.
Has the rock climbing lesson started ___?
items.why: yet goes at the end of questions

items.q: 'I love kayaking,' said Marta. Marta said she ___ kayaking.
items.why: present simple changes to past simple

items.q: 'Put on your helmets,' said the guide. The guide told us ___ our helmets.
items.why: reported order: told us + to + verb

items.q: 'Don't swim here,' said the instructor. He told us ___ there.
'I am scared of heights,' said Leo. Leo said ___ scared of heights.
items.why: I changes to he, am changes to was

items.q: 'We can't go windsurfing,' said the girls. The girls said they ___ go windsurfing.
'I want to try paragliding,' said Sara. Sara said she ___ (want) to try paragliding.
'My brother doesn't like yoga,' said Ben. Ben said his brother ___ (not like) yoga.
items.why: doesn't like changes to didn't like

items.q: 'Wear a life jacket,' the guide told me. The guide told me ___ (wear) a life jacket.
We can't go mountain biking because Dad still ___ (not repair) my bike.
Mum ___ (already book) the kayaks, so we don't need to do it.
items.why: already goes between has and the participle

items.q: Hurry up! The windsurfing class ___ (not start) yet, but it begins in five minutes.
items.why: yet needs the present perfect negative

items.q: I have yet finished my swimming lesson.
a: I have already finished my swimming lesson.
I've already finished my swimming lesson.
I have finished my swimming lesson already.
items.why: affirmative sentences use already, not yet

items.q: She said me that kitesurfing was dangerous.
a: She told me that kitesurfing was dangerous.
She said that kitesurfing was dangerous.
She said to me that kitesurfing was dangerous.
items.why: told + person, or said without a person

items.q: The guide told us don't touch the ropes.
a: The guide told us not to touch the ropes.
items.why: reported negative order: not to + verb

items.q: been / has / my cousin / skydiving / already / twice
a: My cousin has already been skydiving twice.
My cousin has been skydiving twice already.

items.q: said / he / the instructor / tired / that / was
a: The instructor said that he was tired.
He said that the instructor was tired.

units.title: Past continuous
notes: was or were + verb-ing: I was walking. They were visiting the museum.
Negative and questions: She wasn't listening. Were you sleeping?
Use it for an action in progress in the past. A short action in the past simple interrupts it: I was looking at the statue when my phone rang.
Spelling: ride, riding; run, running; sit, sitting.

items.q: At five o'clock yesterday we ___ the palace.
The tourists ___ photos of the monument when it started to rain.
items.why: action in progress in the past

items.q: What ___ your brother doing at the museum yesterday morning?
I ___ listening to the guide, so I got lost in the gallery.
We were looking at the sculpture when the alarm suddenly ___.
items.why: a short, sudden action: past simple

items.q: ___ the workers building the steel bridge last summer?
She was ___ next to the statue when I saw her.
It ___ when we left the tourist information centre, so we didn't need umbrellas.
While the farmers ___ the crops, the children were playing.
At eight o'clock last night I ___ (have) dinner with my family.
items.why: in progress at a past time: was having

items.q: The children ___ (run) around the monument when the guard shouted at them.
My mum ___ (not work) at ten o'clock yesterday morning. She was at home.
I was walking past the glass building when I ___ (see) my teacher.
items.why: the short action is in the past simple

items.q: We ___ (swim) in the sea when the storm began, so we got out quickly.
He broke his arm while he ___ (climb) a brick wall.
They was waiting outside the museum.
a: They were waiting outside the museum.

items.q: I was read a book when you called.
a: I was reading a book when you called.

items.q: What did you doing at six o'clock?
a: What were you doing at six o'clock?
items.why: past continuous questions use was or were

items.q: the palace / when / were / it / we / visiting / started to snow
a: We were visiting the palace when it started to snow.
When it started to snow, we were visiting the palace.

items.q: you / at / what / doing / were / midnight
a: What were you doing at midnight?

units.title: Will for the future; Adverbs of manner
notes: will + base verb for predictions and promises: I think it will rain. I'll help you.
Negative: won't (will not). Questions: Will you come? Yes, I will. No, I won't.
Adverbs of manner say how we do something. Adjective + -ly: quick, quickly; careful, carefully; easy, easily.
Irregular adverbs: good, well; fast, fast; hard, hard: She sings well.

items.q: I think robots ___ all our housework in the future.
Don't worry. I ___ your laptop, I promise.
___ you lend me your charger tomorrow?
items.why: future question: Will + subject + base verb

items.q: Will people live in skyscrapers on the Moon? No, they ___.
My battery is low. It ___ soon.
items.why: will never changes and takes the base verb

items.q: Please type ___. The baby is sleeping.
She plays video games very ___.
items.why: the adverb of good is well

items.q: My grandma types very ___ on her new keyboard. One letter a minute!
He works ___ because he wants to buy a new smartphone.
items.why: hard is irregular; hardly means almost not

items.q: In 2050, I think everybody ___ (have) a robot at home.
items.why: prediction about the future: will + base verb

items.q: I'm sure you ___ (not need) your headphones tomorrow. Leave them at home.
Maybe one day touchscreens ___ (be) as thin as paper.
items.why: one day is the future: will be

items.q: Carry the laptop ___ (careful). It is very expensive.
You can download this app ___ (easy). Just press the button.
items.why: easy: y changes to i, then -ly

items.q: The bulldozer moved ___ (fast) and knocked down the old wall in a minute.
I will to send you the photos tonight.
a: I will send you the photos tonight.
I'll send you the photos tonight.

items.q: She speaks English very good.
items.why: use the adverb well after a verb

items.q: He won't comes to the computer class tomorrow.
a: He won't come to the computer class tomorrow.
He will not come to the computer class tomorrow.

items.q: will / more time / on / I think / spend / social media / people
a: I think people will spend more time on social media.
People will spend more time on social media, I think.

items.q: the mouse / my little sister / slowly / very / moves
a: My little sister moves the mouse very slowly.
items.why: the adverb goes after the object

units.title: First conditional
notes: If + present simple, will + base verb: If we hurry, we will catch the bus.
Use it for possible things in the future.
Never use will after if: If it rains (not if it will rain), we'll stay at home.
The if part can go second, with no comma: I'll buy the tickets if I have enough money.

items.q: Hurry up! If we arrive late tonight, we ___ the start of the concert.
items.why: result in the future: will + base verb

items.q: If the tickets ___ too expensive, we won't go to the opera.
I ___ my guitar if you bring your drums tomorrow.
If she ___ practise the violin, she won't play well in the concert on Friday.
items.why: after if: present simple, she doesn't

items.q: What will you do if the band ___ your favourite song tonight?
If you give up now, you ___ learn to play the saxophone.
___ the audience clap if we play badly on Saturday?
items.why: question about a future result: Will

items.q: We'll get good seats if we ___ early tomorrow.
If Dad ___ the tickets today, we'll see the ballet next week.
items.why: after if: present simple, Dad buys

items.q: If it ___ (rain) tomorrow, the jazz concert will be inside.
Don't worry about tonight's show. If you practise this afternoon, you ___ (play) well.
We ___ (not get) tickets for Saturday's play if we don't book them today.
If my sister ___ (not find) her recorder, she will borrow mine for tomorrow's lesson.
The orchestra will start again if the whole audience ___ (be) quiet.
items.why: present simple after if; audience is singular

items.q: If I save my pocket money this month, I ___ (buy) a trumpet.
If I will see Tom at the concert, I'll say hello.
a: If I see Tom at the concert, I'll say hello.
If I see Tom at the concert, I will say hello.

items.q: If she comes to the ballet, she love it.
a: If she comes to the ballet, she will love it.
If she comes to the ballet, she'll love it.

items.q: We will be late if we doesn't leave now.
a: We will be late if we don't leave now.
We will be late if we do not leave now.

items.q: if / the queue / go home / is / too long / we'll
a: If the queue is too long, we'll go home.
We'll go home if the queue is too long.

items.q: sing / you / with me / if / will / I play / the piano
a: Will you sing with me if I play the piano?
If I play the piano, will you sing with me?
